title: Sinusoids and Complex Exponentials
intro: A sinusoid is fixed by three numbers: how big, how fast and where it starts. Writing it as a turning arrow, $e^{j\omega t}$, packs all three into one complex number and turns the hard parts of trigonometry into arithmetic.

blocks.text: Three numbers
Every pure tone, every hum and every radio carrier has the form

$A$ is the amplitude, the largest value the wave reaches. $f$ is the frequency in hertz, the number of full cycles per second, and $T = 1/f$ is the period, the time one cycle takes. $\varphi$ is the phase, an angle that says where in its cycle the wave is at $t = 0$. Engineers often use angular frequency $\omega = 2\pi f$ in radians per second, which turns the formula into $A\cos(\omega t + \varphi)$; the two are the same wave.

Take $x(t) = 3\cos(2\pi \cdot 5\, t + 60^\circ)$. The amplitude is 3, the frequency 5 Hz, so the period is $1/5 = 0.2$ s. At $t = 0$ the wave is not at its peak but at $3\cos 60^\circ = 1.5$, already on its way down. Its peak came earlier: a phase of $60^\circ$ is $60/360 = 1/6$ of a cycle, so the peak happened $0.2/6 = 0.0333$ s before $t = 0$. A positive phase means the wave leads. Later, at $t = 0.01$ s, it has fallen to $3\cos(18^\circ + 60^\circ) = 0.6237$ (5 Hz for 0.01 s is 0.05 of a cycle, $18^\circ$), and at $t = 0.05$ s, a quarter period after $t = 0$, it is $3\cos(90^\circ + 60^\circ) = -2.5981$.

Three numbers to describe one wave is fine, until you try to add two waves. The sum of two sinusoids of the same frequency is again a sinusoid of that frequency, but finding its amplitude and phase with trigonometric identities is slow and easy to get wrong. The turning arrow removes the effort.
The turning arrow $e^{j\omega t}$

Euler's formula says $e^{j\theta} = \cos\theta + j\sin\theta$. Picture the complex plane: $e^{j\theta}$ is the point on the unit circle at angle $\theta$. Now let the angle grow with time, $\theta = \omega t$. The point runs round the circle at $\omega$ radians per second, counterclockwise, completing $f = \omega/2\pi$ laps every second. That is the turning arrow $e^{j\omega t}$. It has length 1 always, and it carries both parts of a sinusoid: its horizontal shadow is $\cos\omega t$ and its vertical shadow is $\sin\omega t$.

A wave with amplitude and phase is a turning arrow that starts at some angle and has some length. Multiplying by a complex number $A e^{j\varphi}$ does exactly that: it stretches the arrow to length $A$ and rotates it by $\varphi$. So

blocks.tex: A\cos(\omega t + \varphi) = \operatorname{Re}\!\left[\, A e^{j\varphi}\, e^{j\omega t} \right]

blocks.text: The complex number $A e^{j\varphi}$ is called the phasor or complex amplitude. It holds the amplitude and the phase and none of the time dependence. For our example it is $3e^{j60^\circ}$.
Adding waves by adding arrows

Because taking the real part is linear, adding two waves of the same frequency is just adding their phasors. Take $3\cos\omega t - 4\sin\omega t$. The cosine has phasor 3. For the sine, note that $-\sin\omega t = \cos(\omega t + 90^\circ)$, so $-4\sin\omega t$ has phasor $4e^{j90^\circ} = 4j$. The total phasor is $3 + 4j$, which is a 3-4-5 triangle: length 5 and angle $\arctan(4/3) = 53.13^\circ$. So

and we never touched a trigonometric identity. The same method works for any number of waves, so long as they share one frequency. Two waves of different frequencies do not add to a sinusoid at all, which is exactly why the next pages describe a signal as a list of frequencies.

There is a second reason the arrow is the right object. Multiplying two arrows adds their angles, $e^{j\alpha}e^{j\beta} = e^{j(\alpha+\beta)}$, and differentiating one just multiplies it by $j\omega$: $\frac{d}{dt}e^{j\omega t} = j\omega\, e^{j\omega t}$. Calculus on sinusoids becomes multiplication, which is the whole reason the Fourier and Laplace transforms are useful for circuits and vibrations.
A cosine is two arrows
A real signal such as a voltage has no imaginary part, so it cannot be a single arrow. The remedy is to take the arrow and its mirror image. From Euler's formula,

The first formula is two arrows of length $\tfrac12$, one turning counterclockwise at $+\omega$ and one clockwise at $-\omega$. Their vertical parts cancel at every instant and their horizontal parts add, leaving a real wave that swings along the horizontal axis. With an amplitude and a phase,

blocks.tex: A\cos(\omega t + \varphi) = \tfrac{A}{2}e^{j\varphi}\, e^{j\omega t} + \tfrac{A}{2}e^{-j\varphi}\, e^{-j\omega t}

blocks.text: The two coefficients are complex conjugates of each other. For $3\cos(2\pi\cdot 5\,t + 60^\circ)$ the arrow at $+5$ Hz has coefficient $1.5e^{j60^\circ}$ and the one at $-5$ Hz has $1.5e^{-j60^\circ}$.
What a negative frequency is

Negative frequency sounds odd, but it only means a clockwise arrow. The frequency $-5$ Hz is not a different tone from $+5$ Hz that you could hear; it is the same lap rate in the opposite direction. For a real signal the two always come as a conjugate pair, so the negative half carries no new information. It is bookkeeping that keeps the arithmetic clean, and the Fourier transform of a real signal is always symmetric: $X(-f) = \overline{X(f)}$, its magnitude even and its phase odd. The Reading a Spectrum (#/math/fourier-transform/spectrum) page returns to this when it compares one-sided and two-sided spectra.

A complex signal such as $e^{j2\pi\cdot 3t}$ does tell the two directions apart. Its real part is the same as that of $e^{-j2\pi\cdot 3t}$, but its imaginary part has the opposite sign. Radio engineers use complex signals for exactly this reason: a single arrow can say 'three hertz above the carrier' where a real wave cannot tell above from below.
Try it: two tones

The viewer below starts with the signal named two tones, $\cos(\omega_0 t) + 0.5\cos(3\omega_0 t + 60^\circ)$, which is two sinusoids and nothing else. Each is a ribbon at its own frequency in the 3D view, and the dark curve in front is their sum.

Leave Harmonics added at 3 and read the readout line under the picture: k = 1 has amplitude 1 and phase 0, k = 3 has amplitude 0.5 and phase 60 degrees, and nothing else exists. Turn the view to Turn −90 and Tilt 10 to see only the spectrum: two stems, at 1 Hz and 3 Hz. Now raise Delay to 0.1. The amplitudes do not change, but the phase panel moves the two lines to −36° and −48°. Delaying a wave by a tenth of a period rotates each arrow back by a tenth of its own turn, and the third harmonic turns three times as fast: $-36^\circ \times 3 = -108^\circ$, and $60^\circ - 108^\circ = -48^\circ$.
Practice

blocks.title: Read off the three numbers
blocks.text: A signal is $2\cos(40\pi t - 30^\circ)$. Find its frequency, its period and its value at $t = 0$.
solution: Compare with $A\cos(2\pi f t + \varphi)$: $2\pi f = 40\pi$, so $f = 20$ Hz and $T = 1/20 = 0.05$ s. The amplitude is 2 and the phase $-30^\circ$, so the wave lags. At $t = 0$ it is $2\cos(-30^\circ) = 2 \times 0.8660 = 1.7321$.

blocks.title: Add two waves
blocks.text: Add $2\cos\omega t$ and $2\cos(\omega t + 120^\circ)$ with phasors.
solution: The phasors are $2$ and $2e^{j120^\circ} = 2(-0.5 + 0.8660j) = -1 + 1.7321j$. Their sum is $1 + 1.7321j$, with length $\sqrt{1 + 3} = 2$ and angle $\arctan(1.7321/1) = 60^\circ$. So the sum is $2\cos(\omega t + 60^\circ)$: two waves of amplitude 2, $120^\circ$ apart, add to a wave of amplitude 2, half-way between them.

blocks.title: Sine as two arrows
blocks.text: Write $5\sin\omega t$ as a sum of two complex exponentials.
solution: Use $\sin\theta = (e^{j\theta} - e^{-j\theta})/2j$. Then $5\sin\omega t = \frac{5}{2j}e^{j\omega t} - \frac{5}{2j}e^{-j\omega t}$. Since $1/j = -j$, the coefficient at $+\omega$ is $-2.5j$ and the one at $-\omega$ is $+2.5j$. They are complex conjugates, as they must be for a real signal, and each has length 2.5, half the amplitude.

blocks.title: Which way does it turn?
blocks.text: The signals $e^{j2\pi\cdot 3t}$ and $e^{-j2\pi\cdot 3t}$ have the same real part. How do they differ, and what does their sum look like?
solution: The first is $\cos(6\pi t) + j\sin(6\pi t)$ and the second $\cos(6\pi t) - j\sin(6\pi t)$. The real parts are equal; the imaginary parts are opposite, so one arrow turns counterclockwise and the other clockwise. Adding them cancels the imaginary parts and doubles the real part: $2\cos(6\pi t)$, a real 3 Hz wave.
blocks.answer: Same real part, opposite imaginary parts; the sum is $2\cos 6\pi t$.
